title: Non-specific Low Back Pain
case: Case: A 38-year-old delivery driver has 3 weeks of central low back pain after lifting boxes. Pain is worse bending forward and sitting long, easier walking. No leg symptoms, normal reflexes, negative SLR, no red flags. Prone press-ups reduce his pain and it stays reduced afterwards. He worries that his back is damaged.

Working diagnosis: non-specific mechanical low back pain with a possible extension directional preference. Plan: explain the favourable outlook, press-ups several times a day, walking, short driving breaks, progressive lifting practice, reassess in a week.
qa: Why is a scan not needed here? Imaging rarely changes management in flag-free back pain, and many scan findings also occur in people without symptoms [Ref - to verify].
Why discuss his fear? Fear of damage can lead to avoiding movement, which may prolong disability [Ref - to verify].
What would make you change the plan today? Saddle numbness, bladder change, leg weakness or spreading leg pain. Any of these means stop and use the Section G or Ch 2 pathway.
The press-ups make leg pain worse after 10 repetitions. What next? Stop that direction because symptoms are peripheralising, then test another movement or manage via Ch 2.
Why is TENS not chosen as the main treatment? Evidence shows little added benefit for most patients and it does not address movement or function.

fields.Purpose: Find out whether repeated movement in one direction changes symptoms in a lasting and useful way (directional preference)
fields.Action: Ask the patient to do 10 repetitions of one movement, for example prone press-ups (lying on the stomach, pushing the upper body up with the arms). Record pain location before, during and after
fields.Positive (useful response): Pain moves from the leg or buttock toward the centre of the back (centralisation), or pain decreases and range increases and the improvement lasts after the movement
fields.Negative: Pain increases, spreads further away, or does not change
fields.Supports: A direction of movement that may suit exercise treatment
fields.Limits: It does not identify a specific structure. Evidence for MDT is mixed [Ref - to verify]
fields.Errors: Too few repetitions; not recording pain location; continuing when symptoms move further down the leg
fields.Next step: If a direction helps, use it as a home exercise. If symptoms peripheralise (spread away from the spine) stop that direction

fields.Purpose: Check whether pain eased by muscle activation suggests a movement-control problem
fields.Position: Prone with the trunk on the bench and feet on the floor
fields.Action: Step 1: apply posterior-to-anterior pressure over each lumbar segment and note pain. Step 2: ask the patient to lift the feet off the floor to activate the back muscles, and repeat the pressure
fields.Positive: Pain present at rest but reduced or gone when the muscles are active
fields.Supports: May suggest a benefit from motor control exercise. Not proof of instability
fields.Limits: Reliability and meaning are debated [Ref - to verify]

redFlags.Finding: Saddle numbness or tingling, new bladder or bowel dysfunction, new sexual dysfunction
redFlags.Why it matters: Compression of the lower nerve roots
redFlags.Immediate action: Stop; same-day hospital emergency referral. Do not wait to see if it improves

redFlags.Finding: Bilateral leg pain or weakness with progression
Major trauma, or minor trauma with older age, osteoporosis or long-term steroid use
redFlags.Immediate action: Do not load; refer for imaging

redFlags.Finding: Fever, recent infection, intravenous drug use, immune suppression with back pain
Past cancer, unexplained weight loss, age over 50 with new constant pain, night pain
Sudden severe back or abdominal pain with a pulsatile abdominal feeling, older patient

manual.name: Graded mobilization of lumbar or thoracic spine
manual.why: May give short-term pain relief and make movement easier [Ref - to verify]
manual.finding: Stiff painful segment, patient prefers hands-on
manual.application: Prone, central or unilateral postero-anterior glides, low to moderate grade, 30 to 60 seconds per segment
manual.stop: Leg symptoms spread; increased pain after treatment

manual.name: Spinal manipulation
manual.why: Option for short-term relief in some patients [Ref - to verify]
manual.finding: No red flags, no nerve compromise, patient consents

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education and active movement first. Manual therapy is an optional adjunct used mainly for short-term relief. Do not claim that it realigns the spine or fixes a disc.

Is it working? Look for greater range, easier function and the patient's own rating of change over the same session and the next session. If no benefit after a few sessions, stop and choose another approach.

exercise.Progress when: Can increase time without lasting flare
exercise.Regress when: Pain flares for more than a day

exercise.Steps: Lying on the back with knees bent, rock the pelvis
On hands and knees, round then arch gently
On hands and knees, extend opposite arm and leg

exercise.Starting dose: 10 reps, a few times a day

exerciseNotes: Symptom rule: discomfort during exercise that settles within a short time is acceptable. Pain spreading into the leg, new numbness or weakness means stop and reassess. This is an example, not a protocol. Different exercise types (strengthening, motor control, aerobic, mixed) seem to help to a similar degree [Ref - to verify], so choose according to patient preference, tolerance and goals.

modalities.name: TENS
modalities.indicated: Not routinely recommended in several guidelines [Ref - to verify]
modalities.comment: May be used for comfort if the patient likes it

pathway: Any emergency flag? Yes: emergency action.
Any urgent flag? Yes: defer treatment and refer.
Leg pain below the knee with root signs? Yes: go to Ch 2.

Mechanical back pain, no nerve signs, no flags? Yes: working diagnosis is non-specific low back pain. Stratify risk (for example with the STarT Back Screening Tool [Ref - to verify]) to decide how much support is needed.
No flags but unusually high disability or distress? Add psychosocial strategies and consider combined care.
Visit 1: screen flags, examine, explain that serious causes are unlikely if flags are negative, give honest but positive expectations, advise to stay active.
Early: reduce fear, gentle movement, short walks, sleep and work advice, optional manual therapy.
Middle: progress exercise, add strength and function-based work.
